lessons.title: Making inferences from a text
lessons.description: Combine details in a text with what you already know to draw a careful inference.
lessons.content: An inference is a reasonable conclusion that is not stated word for word. A reader uses clues in the text and relevant prior knowledge. An inference must be supported by evidence, not by a guess.
learning_objectives: Explain the difference between a stated fact and an inference.
Use textual clues to support an inference.
Avoid conclusions that go beyond available evidence.
prerequisites: Identify key details in a short paragraph.

explanation_sections.title: Clue plus reasoning
explanation_sections.body: Read the passage carefully, identify a clue, then explain how it supports your conclusion. If a passage says the ground is wet and learners carry umbrellas, rain is a reasonable inference. The passage does not prove exactly when the rain fell.

explanation_sections.title: Check your inference
explanation_sections.body: Ask whether the text supports your idea and whether another explanation is possible. Strong readers separate what the author states directly from what the clues suggest.

worked_examples.prompt: A story says that Nia packed a water bottle, a hat and a map before leaving for a long walk. What can you infer?
worked_examples.solution: Nia is preparing for an outdoor walk or journey.
worked_examples.reasoning: The map and walking supplies are clues. They support preparation for a journey but do not prove the exact destination.

lessons.author: ElimuQuest Curriculum Team

questions.prompt: A passage says, 'The path was muddy, and Kamau wiped his shoes at the door.' Which inference is best supported?
options: Kamau probably walked on a wet path.
Kamau bought new shoes that morning.
questions.correct_answer: Kamau probably walked on a wet path.
questions.explanation: Mud on the path and shoes is evidence of a recent walk on wet ground. The other claims are not supported.

questions.prompt: What makes an inference different from a directly stated fact?
options: An inference is a conclusion drawn from clues.
An inference is always a character's opinion.
A fact cannot be checked in a text.
A fact is based only on imagination.
questions.correct_answer: An inference is a conclusion drawn from clues.
questions.explanation: A direct fact is stated; an inference is reasoned from details and knowledge.

questions.prompt: A learner concludes that a character is tired because the text says the character yawned repeatedly and struggled to keep their eyes open. What is the strongest evidence?
options: The character's repeated yawning and difficulty staying awake.
questions.correct_answer: The character's repeated yawning and difficulty staying awake.
questions.explanation: Those details directly support the inference that the character is tired.

lessons.title: Writing a coherent paragraph
lessons.description: Organise a paragraph around one main point and connect each detail to it.
lessons.content: A clear paragraph develops one main point. A topic sentence introduces that point, supporting sentences explain it with reasons or examples, and a closing sentence can bring the idea together.
learning_objectives: Write a topic sentence that states one main point.
Choose supporting details that relate to the main point.
Use linking words to show how ideas connect.
prerequisites: Write complete sentences with correct punctuation.

explanation_sections.title: Plan before writing
explanation_sections.body: Decide what the paragraph should explain. Write the main point in one sentence, then list two or three details that support it. Remove a detail that belongs to a different topic.

explanation_sections.title: Use linking words
explanation_sections.body: Words such as because, for example, however and therefore show relationships between ideas. Choose a linking word that matches the relationship; do not add one just to make the paragraph sound longer.

worked_examples.prompt: Make these ideas into a focused paragraph plan: 'A school garden is useful. Learners observe plant growth. They practise teamwork. A football match has two teams.'
worked_examples.solution: Topic sentence: A school garden supports learning. Supporting details: learners observe plant growth and practise teamwork.
worked_examples.reasoning: The football-match detail is about another subject, so it does not support the paragraph's main point.

lessons.author: ElimuQuest Curriculum Team

questions.prompt: Which sentence best introduces a paragraph about the benefits of reading daily?
options: Reading every day can build knowledge and vocabulary.
questions.correct_answer: Reading every day can build knowledge and vocabulary.
questions.explanation: It states a central point that can be supported with relevant examples.

questions.prompt: Which detail best supports the topic sentence 'Planning helps learners complete assignments on time'?
options: A written plan divides a large task into smaller steps with due dates.
questions.correct_answer: A written plan divides a large task into smaller steps with due dates.
questions.explanation: The detail explains how planning can help finish work on schedule.

questions.prompt: Which linking word best completes the sentence? 'The team practised regularly; _____, its performance improved.'
questions.explanation: Therefore introduces a result of the regular practice.
